title: Learning sparse linear state-space models
one_liner: Recover the true sparse structure of variables in time-series data by penalizing unnecessary connections during learning.
lead: Time-series data (stock prices, weather, sensor readings) often come from systems where only a few variables influence each other; most pairs are unrelated. Classical learning algorithms overfit by finding connections everywhere, even noise. This paper recovers the true sparse structure by gently steering the learning process to prefer simpler, sparser connection patterns.

problem.h2: Why sparse structures matter and why learning fails to find them
paras: Imagine measuring temperature, humidity, and wind speed over 100 days. Temperature affects humidity. Wind affects temperature. But humidity does not affect wind. The system is sparse: only some pairs have real connections.

A beginner might train a model to predict the next hour's readings from the current hour. A naive learner will find spurious connections, especially in noisy data where random coincidences look like real relationships. It treats all pairs equally and overfits, learning noise instead of the true three-connection structure. Predictions drift.

The reason: standard algorithms treat the system as a black box. They do not prefer sparse solutions. When two explanations fit the data equally well—one with 3 connections and one with 30—they pick based on noise alone, not structure.

callout.html: Add a penalty for unnecessary connections so the learning algorithm prefers simpler, sparser systems that actually match the data's true causal structure.

steps.text: Set up a prior (initial belief) that most connections are zero or very small.
Cycle: guess hidden states from data, then update connection strengths toward nonzero connections only.
After each update, reduce small connection values toward zero, shrinking the model.
Repeat until only strong connections survive and predictions stabilize.
The final model retains the true causal skeleton of the system.

paras: The paper changes a single thing: it adds a sparsity penalty (a cost) to the learning process. This penalty makes the algorithm pay a price for each connection it learns, so it only keeps connections that strongly improve predictions. Weak or spurious connections get eliminated.

hidden.name: sparsity strength
paras: Sparsity strength is how aggressively the algorithm penalizes connections. Imagine tuning a dial: turn it to zero and you get classical overfitting (all 30 connections learned). Turn it up and the algorithm increasingly eliminates weak connections. Very high, and you get a nearly empty system.

The paper estimates this strength by looking at which connections survive repeated EM cycles without shrinking to zero. Connections that persist through many iterations are data-driven; those that vanish were noise-driven artifacts. The EM algorithm itself discovers the right strength automatically by maximizing likelihood while respecting the sparsity prior.

heat.caption: Darker means this connection survived the sparsity penalty; lighter ones got eliminated.

reads.html: Sparsity strength is how much we penalize making new connections. It is the dial that controls whether to keep or discard weak links.

In the EM framework, sparsity strength is the hyperparameter in the sparsity-promoting prior. The paper derives it from the data via maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimation, letting the likelihood and prior balance automatically.

mechanism.h2: Why the method works: the learning path
paras: The mechanism is a two-stage loop. First, the EM algorithm fills in hidden states (the unmeasured internal values) based on what it knows so far. Second, it updates the connection strengths to best predict the data. Normally, this update tries to fit everything—signal and noise. But here, it also subtracts a penalty: cost per connection. That cost biases the update away from weak links and toward strong ones.

Over many iterations, weak connections (which don't earn back their cost) shrink to near zero. Strong, data-driven connections persist because they reduce prediction error more than their penalty costs. The result: the algorithm naturally converges to the true sparse structure, not a dense overfitted one. The theory (Global Convergence Theorem) guarantees the iterates do not bounce around forever; they settle on a real local optimum.

math.h2: The equation: likelihood plus sparsity penalty
math.words: Total cost = negative log-likelihood of the data plus lambda times sum of absolute values of connections
symbols: The total cost we minimize (lower is better)
How well the connection strengths theta explain the observed data y
The sparsity strength dial: how much to penalize each connection
The sum of absolute sizes of all connection values; penalizes any connection that exists

worked.title: A tiny worked example with two connections
lines: Suppose two connections have strengths theta_1 = 0.8 and theta_2 = 0.1.
Suppose lambda (sparsity penalty) = 1.0, and the data-fit term says 'theta_1 = 0.8 is worth keeping' but 'theta_2 = 0.1 barely helps'.
Cost for theta_1: data-fit gain (large) minus penalty 1.0 * |0.8| = 0.8. Net gain: big minus small.
Cost for theta_2: data-fit gain (tiny) minus penalty 1.0 * |0.1| = 0.1. Net gain: small minus small, nearly zero.
In the next EM iteration, the algorithm shrinks theta_2 because its penalty erodes any benefit. theta_1 survives because it earns back the cost.

math.note: Higher lambda (stricter penalty) gives sparser models; lower lambda gives denser, more overfit models. EM automatically finds the right balance.

charts.title: Naive algorithm (no sparsity)
charts.note: Overfits to noise; many spurious connections; fails on new data.

charts.title: This paper (with sparsity)
charts.note: Training fit drops slightly (88 vs 92) because the sparsity penalty prevents overfitting to noise, but new-data predictions jump from 56 to 81 because the learned system is now closer to the true structure. The sparse model avoids memorizing noise-driven spurious connections, because the EM algorithm prefers to drop a weak connection and accept slightly lower training accuracy if keeping it costs more in sparsity penalty than it gains in prediction error.

items.html: If lambda is too small, the algorithm still overfits and learns spurious connections. The penalty must hurt enough to discourage weak links.
If lambda is too large, even important connections get eliminated. Predictions collapse because the system becomes too simple.
If EM gets stuck in a bad local optimum early on (wrong guess about unmeasured values), it may never recover the true structure.
The paper's EM formulation with sparsity priors lets the data and prior balance automatically. No manual tuning; the algorithm discovers the right lambda from the joint posterior.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate synthetic time-series data from a known sparse system (e.g., three variables, three real connections, plus random noise). Run the paper's EM algorithm with sparsity priors. Also run a naive algorithm without sparsity. Compare: (1) how many of the three true connections does each recover? (2) how many false connections does each learn? (3) on held-out test data, which model predicts better? The sparse model wins because the sparsity penalty prevents the algorithm from chasing down noise-driven spurious connections—only true connections pull their weight against the penalty cost. The naive model, lacking this penalty, fits every coincidence in the training data, so those coincidences vanish on new data. Structure recovery demonstrates the mechanism: sparsity priors survive only strong data-driven connections.
demo.metric_eq: Structure recovery = (true connections found) / (true connections total). Generalization = test-set prediction error. Sparsity = number of nonzero connections learned.
demo.closing: The sparse model should recover all three true connections, learn zero false ones, and predict better on new data. This proves that sparsity priors survive only data-driven connections and eliminate noise-driven overfitting, because the cost of keeping weak connections outweighs any random fitting gain.
